1173b86c-adcb-5487-87ea-85f5d2fd9b53.title: Water as Sacred Presence: Gardens, Paradise, and Salvation
1173b86c-adcb-5487-87ea-85f5d2fd9b53.quote: Inspired by Quranic visions of paradise, water shaped Islamic visual culture through gardens, fountains, ceramic tiles, and carpets. Flowing channels and lush landscapes translated sacred imagery into artistic forms that evoke beauty, harmony, and divine reward.

2a31b6e0-43fa-5b33-af86-569f085568d3.title: Domestic Hygiene
2a31b6e0-43fa-5b33-af86-569f085568d3.quote: Cleanliness holds deep spiritual meaning in Islam, where disciplined bodily purification through *al-wudu* and *ghusl* is closely tied to purification of the soul. Water, as the medium of this renewal, shaped the architecture of baths, courtyards, and washing spaces within the home. Its intimate presence in daily life expressed faith’s close connections among discipline, purity, order, and well-being.

367a1ed0-0e57-5a75-aae5-0a83f8f0367c.title: Contemporary Context: Water in the Islamic World Today
367a1ed0-0e57-5a75-aae5-0a83f8f0367c.presentation:
This theme examines water as an ethical, technical, symbolic and artistic element in modern Islam. Islamic environmental ethics understand water through the concept of *khalifa*, which defines humans as God’s trustees and caretakers on Earth. This principle promotes stewardship through sustainable practices, including garden reconstruction, communal water management and the preservation of traditional meanings of water through local museums and heritage initiatives.*Khalifa* connects traditional and modern water systems, such as *aflaj* and contemporary infrastructure. It has remained constant across the Muslim world even as methods of collecting, storing and distributing water evolve.  
  
Urban transformation demonstrates water’s material and symbolic significance. Streets, so central to the urban landscape, and infrastructure such as parks, water towers and hammams, are shaped by systems of water distribution and sale. Water engineering is also present in visual culture, from banknotes to contemporary art, conveying themes of purity, life and prosperity.  
  
Within this context, the water crisis exposes significant inequalities. Arid regions face severe access challenges, rural communities experience unequal extraction and distribution and climate change increases scarcity and pollution. In the Middle East, armed conflicts further worsen water insecurity by damaging infrastructure and further limiting access. These issues are reflected in cultural expressions and visual art that highlights the historical and cultural significance of water in Islamic culture.

36b99d7f-1117-5074-a5ac-d49177ae0f4d.title: Water in Human Creativity: Literature, Poetry, and Epics
36b99d7f-1117-5074-a5ac-d49177ae0f4d.quote: In Islamic literature, water serves as a powerful metaphor in poetry and epics. Rivers, springs, and seas signify love and separation, luxury and illusion, reflecting the shifting emotions and moral complexities of human experience.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b.title: Rivers of Life: Agriculture Along the Great Waterways
4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b.quote: The rivers carried more than water — they carried knowledge, power, and prosperity. Along their banks, Islamic civilisation cultivated landscapes that fed cities, moved markets, and transformed the world.

4e8133ba-b181-554a-bd52-4bf13639f568.title: Water in Knowledge, Science, and Technology
4e8133ba-b181-554a-bd52-4bf13639f568.quote: In Islamic intellectual traditions, water inspired scientific inquiry and innovation. Scholars and engineers studied its movement and power, developing navigation tools, maps, irrigation systems, and hydraulic machines that supported travel, trade, and life.

5c132532-2bdd-5527-aa0b-3f55c3a5d81f.title: Islamic Environmental Ethics and Stewardship
5c132532-2bdd-5527-aa0b-3f55c3a5d81f.quote: Within Islamic thought, water management combines technical expertise and ethical considerations with scientific understanding and spiritual insight. "The Muslims are partners in three things: water, pasture and fire, and their price is unlawful." (Sunan Ibn Majah 2472)

5e107040-dcc0-547b-91d1-5e7258472080.title: Water and the Human Condition: Prophets, Saints, and Sinners
5e107040-dcc0-547b-91d1-5e7258472080.quote: In Islamic sacred narratives, water mediates divine trial and grace. It marks moments of testing, repentance, and transformation, embodying both punishment and mercy, and reflecting the moral tension among error, patience, and redemption.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0.title: Engineering the Flow: Irrigation Technologies and Water Management
6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0.quote: To make water flow was to master survival. Across centuries and continents, Islamic ingenuity turned ancient techniques into living systems, where engineering met equity, and nature met knowledge.

659b895d-1c67-583f-8d27-8170d5b1d7c3.title: "The Best Charity is a Drink of Water" (Hadith: Sunan An-Nasa'i 3694)
659b895d-1c67-583f-8d27-8170d5b1d7c3.quote: The Architecture of Mercy: Endowments and Public Welfare

6b701948-1e27-542e-a3fb-9f27270569b8.title: Water in Gardens
6b701948-1e27-542e-a3fb-9f27270569b8.quote: In the Quran, gardens are a vision of paradise on earth — a space where the spiritual and natural worlds meet through the movement of water. Streams, basins, and channels shaped garden sanctuaries by offering sensory pleasure and spiritual meaning. The rhythmic sound of flowing water encouraged contemplation, while its presence mirrored divine order, balance, and eternal renewal within the cultivated harmony of nature.  Gardens are also the ultimate reward for the righteous believer: “Allah has promised the believers, both men and women, Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay there forever, and splendid homes in the Gardens of Eternity, and—above all—the pleasure of Allah. That is 'truly' the ultimate triumph.” – Quran 9:72

6df2d667-393f-56fd-ac89-764ecf509141.title: Transport
6df2d667-393f-56fd-ac89-764ecf509141.quote: The journey of water from source to household was a testament to human ingenuity and adaptation. Through channels, ceramic pipes, and bronze containers, communities devised sophisticated methods to transport water from its sources to urban centres and domestic settings.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c.title: Roots in the Sand: Oasis Agriculture and the Origin of Islamic Farming
71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c.quote: From the harshest environments, Islamic civilisation nurtured thriving agricultural systems. Oasis farming, born of necessity, became a symbol of sustainability, cooperation, and ingenuity. It reminds us that life, when guided by water and community, can flourish even in the desert.

80cd42c3-f130-56d3-b0fc-8a033ff888a2.title: The Symbolism of Water in sacred Texts, secular Literature, and Science
80cd42c3-f130-56d3-b0fc-8a033ff888a2.presentation:
In Islamic thought, water (*ma*) is a foundational element of both spiritual belief and human knowledge. It is mentioned more than 70 times across the Quran, where it signifies the origin of life, divine mercy, and a medium through which God tests, guides, and transforms humankind. Paradise itself is repeatedly imagined through water-filled imagery—'*gardens beneath which rivers flow*'—while *janna* and *jannat*, mentioned over 100 times, are promised as eternal reward for believers (e.g., 2:25; 47:15). Sacred waters such as the river of al-Kawthar (108:1) and the Zamzam wellspring embody divine generosity, healing, and protection, while ritual purification through *wudu* and *tahara* affirms water’s essential role in cleansing body and soul.  
  
Prophetic narratives reveal water’s dual nature as mercy and punishment. In the story of Jonah (Yunus), cast into the sea and swallowed by the whale (21:87; 37:139–148), water becomes the site of divine trial and forgiveness, where patience and repentance lead to salvation. The flood of Noah (*nuh*), recounted in an entire Quranic chapter (71) and elsewhere (11:40–44), similarly reflects destruction and renewal, affirming divine justice and mercy through water.  
  
Beyond sacred texts, water flows through Islamic literature as a metaphor for love, separation, power, and illusion. In works such as the '*Khamsa'* of Nizami, the '*Bustan*', '*Mantiq al-Tayr*', and '*Iskandarnama*', springs and rivers divide or unite lovers, mark scenes of courtly luxury, or symbolise the elusive search for eternal life, as in Alexander’s quest for the Water of Life and its association with *al-Khidr*. In fables like '*Kalila wa Dimna*', water embodies wisdom and deception, capable of saving or destroying those who misread its nature.  
  
Water also stands at the heart of knowledge, science, and technological innovation. While the sea evokes fear and danger, it also reflects the infinity of God’s words (18:109). The sea became a pathway for travel, trade, and empires. Muslim societies mastered shipbuilding and navigation, developing astrolabes, celestial globes, star charts, and maps, while linking cosmology to water through constellations such as Pisces and Aquarius. Engineers and scholars advanced hydraulic sciences, designing irrigation systems, measuring devices, and water-powered machines that sustained cities and landscapes across the Islamic world, many of which endure to this day.

949af30f-e113-501b-8cea-ba30237d2ecd.title: Religion and Spirituality
949af30f-e113-501b-8cea-ba30237d2ecd.presentation:
In the Islamic tradition, water (maʾ) is a sacred trust that accompanies the believer from birth to the grave. The Qur’an highlights this spiritual quality, stating: “And We sent down from the sky purifying water” (25:48). This theological foundation establishes water as the primary medium of moral order, where the physical act of washing becomes a spiritual transformation. Through the rituals of ablution (*wudu*) and ritual bath (*ghusl*), the believer prepares for prayer by entering a state of sacred presence, fulfilling the Prophetic teaching that “Purity is half of faith”. This journey of purification concludes at the end of life with ghusl al-mayyit, where the ritual washing of the deceased serves as a final act of dignity and respect.  
  
The spiritual life of water also demands ethical stewardship because, as the scripture reminds us, “We sent down water from the sky in measure” (23:18). Its preservation is a religious mandate, reflected in the communal prayer for rain (*salat al-istisqa*) and the sophisticated engineering of aqueducts and measuring vessels designed to prevent waste (*israf*).  
  
This importance is further reflected in architecture and the spatial organisation of the community. In many mosques, courtyards include pools or fountains for ablution, integrating ritual preparation into the physical building. Beyond the mosque, public water structures such as sabils provided drinking water as charitable endowments supported through the institution of *waqf*. Bathhouses (hammams) served both hygienic and social functions, while inscriptions on fountains and endowment plaques record the names of patrons who established these facilities. These structures embody the Prophetic tradition that “the best charity is a drink of water”, turning water provision into a lasting legacy of public welfare and divine service.

981d7f37-ff97-5e15-936b-4b7fe274ae4a.title: Water as Source of Healing, Life, and Protection
981d7f37-ff97-5e15-936b-4b7fe274ae4a.quote: Across Islamic belief and practice, water sustains life and safeguards the body and soul. Sacred springs, ritual purification, and blessed waters affirm its role as a source of healing, protection, and spiritual renewal.

a9af03e0-1b2c-5d10-b279-d1dc98fd209f.title: "We Sent Down Water in Measure" (23:18)
a9af03e0-1b2c-5d10-b279-d1dc98fd209f.quote: Divine Equilibrium: Stewardship, Measurement, and Justice

aff608af-f2c7-54b7-8325-794e1d8d4ba1.title: Urban Water Infrastructure
aff608af-f2c7-54b7-8325-794e1d8d4ba1.quote: Water shaped the fabric of urban life through aqueducts, *sabils*, fountains, and subterranean channels. These networks not only sustained cities, but they embodied ideals of generosity and civic ingenuity.

b81c7cb9-ba05-562a-a64d-68b2e17400e0.title: About
b81c7cb9-ba05-562a-a64d-68b2e17400e0.presentation:
This exhibition explores the central role of water in Islamic civilisation, presenting it as the origin of life, a sign of divine mercy, and a shared ethical trust. In Islamic thought, water is not merely a resource but a formative force that shaped agriculture, urban development, ritual practice, artistic expression, and scientific inquiry.  
  
Bringing together objects, monuments and narratives from multiple regions, it examines water’s material, spiritual and symbolic dimensions, from purification and sacred spaces to literature, technology and environmental reflection. Structured around five interconnected themes, the exhibition links historical experience with contemporary concerns such as sustainability, coexistence and stewardship.  
  
Reflecting MWNF’s multicultural vision, the exhibition brings together an international community of scholars and partner institutions, building bridges across cultures through shared heritage and knowledge.

c313de84-08f6-5017-93b2-06aba8eeb41a.title: Household Tools
c313de84-08f6-5017-93b2-06aba8eeb41a.quote: From humble clay jars to ornate metal ewers, the objects designed to carry water reveal a dialogue between function and artistry. Crafted with care and beauty, these vessels are tangible reminders of the daily rituals of hospitality, hygiene, and devotion that structured domestic life. Their materials and forms vary across regions, yet each embodies an enduring respect for water as both a physical necessity and a spiritual blessing.

cf106957-b4e8-5d72-9a13-749b82c4b545.title: Water and Agriculture in Islamic Civilisation
cf106957-b4e8-5d72-9a13-749b82c4b545.presentation:
Agriculture played an important role in economic and urban development in Islamic civilisation. The spread of Islam produced substantial development in agriculture in the diversification of crops; regulations and laws; water management; and agricultural techniques.  
  
Islamic civilisation spread over a vast geographical area from Andalusia on the Iberian Peninsula to Central Asia, in different geographical, climatic, historical and social settings. Methods of irrigation and water management were employed based on the varied settings of regions and areas.  
  
Although agricultural techniques are often inherited from former civilisations, advances during the spread of Islam were notable. Techniques for water management were upgraded, transferred from region to region, and maintained, leading to increased productivity.  
Agriculture affected the urban development of several areas through access to water. One example is Yazid City in Iran, developed via the *qanat* system of transporting water. The change from planting one crop per year to multiple crops had an impact on social life as well.  
  
Advances in legal regulations on the use of water and ownership of land made a great difference in the evolution of agriculture.

d9892ae7-847a-57c8-bac6-b4d4da472117.title: Traditional and Modern Water Systems
d9892ae7-847a-57c8-bac6-b4d4da472117.quote: Today, water systems diversity reflects rapid societal change. In rural areas, traditional infrastructure remains largely unchanged, while urban settings adapt ancient engineering to meet modern needs.

dcde71d1-a00d-5854-af52-7562c71ef203.title: Water Crisis and Inequality
dcde71d1-a00d-5854-af52-7562c71ef203.quote: Muslim-majority regions from North Africa to South Asia experience significant water stress due to climate change, deteriorating infrastructure, unsustainable water consumption and ongoing geopolitical conflict.

dd084451-a673-5a08-9e5c-1511b897833e.title: Art and Water, Contemporary Approach
dd084451-a673-5a08-9e5c-1511b897833e.quote: "In Islamic art today, water remains both material and metaphor – fluid pigment, dissolving boundary and bearer of memory." Sultan Sooud Al-Qassemi, Barjeel Art Foundation

eb0a0f58-72d0-5c98-a5dc-283759eac032.title: Gardens of Knowledge: Agricultural Science and the Scholars of Water
eb0a0f58-72d0-5c98-a5dc-283759eac032.quote: "Islamic scholars cultivated fields of knowledge as carefully as they did the land, blending science, skill, and sustainability into a living legacy."

ebf15498-6f84-536b-aac4-f726dd74ced5.title: Domestic and Urban Spheres
ebf15498-6f84-536b-aac4-f726dd74ced5.presentation:
In Islam, water plays a crucial role in a Muslim’s spiritual and physical life. For instance, water is essential for daily ablutions (*al-wudu*) before prayers and the full-body cleansing (*ghusl*).  
  
In addition to these ritual dimensions, water played a fundamental role in shaping urban networks across the medieval Islamic world. Water’s movement and distribution — through repositories such as aqueducts, cisterns, channels and urban waterways — defined the rhythm of daily life. On a macro scale, within mosques, private homes and gardens, water created spaces of comfort and reflection, echoing Quranic imagery of paradise (*janna*) and renewal. Islam also emphasises the equitable distribution and conservation of water. Giving water to the thirsty is considered a highly-rewarded act of charity (*sadaqa*).  
  
Beyond these practical and spiritual uses, water also shaped quotidian objects. The tools and vessels designed to store and dispense water, including in public baths (*hammam*), are an indication of sophisticated craftsmanship manifested variously in different regions, bridging functionality and artistic expression.

f45fdab9-b22d-5759-be60-cc34bf79daa8.title: "Purity is Half of Faith" (Hadith: Sahih Muslim 432)
f45fdab9-b22d-5759-be60-cc34bf79daa8.quote: The Moral Order: Ritual Transformation & Liminal Space

f9092d23-3069-5905-aa85-7a774bee0ab1.title: Urban Transformation and Symbolism
f9092d23-3069-5905-aa85-7a774bee0ab1.quote: "Islamic urbanism is not static but rhythmic, it renews itself while preserving its spiritual proportions." — Spahic Omer, Muslim Architecture: Form, Function and Meaning

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/bd0.contextual_description: Islamic civilisation promoted the fair use of water and the rights of access to it. Particularly where water was rare, the concept was of crucial importance. Figuig Oasis in Morocco demonstrates fair water use in oases. It comprises seven villages, each with its own water sources and irrigation systems. They all follow the same rules for sharing water based on time allocation. Water was divided to allow its use based on need. This system began in pre-Islamic times and became more organised during the early Muslim dynasties.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/3db.contextual_description: A symbol of water heritage, the water clock is used in the oases of southeastern Morocco, particularly in Tafilalet, to measure irrigation turns. Farmers rely on it to know exactly how long they can access water. It has deep cultural meanings, reflecting the sanctity of water-sharing, and is a powerful symbol of Morocco’s living hydraulic heritage and community self-governance.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/ca2.contextual_description: Rooted in Moroccan water law, the *maada* reflects principles of equity, transparency and shared responsibility in agricultural water management. It is used to distribute irrigation water fairly among users, as it carefully measures outflows that correspond to established rights defined by custom and law.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/2bb.contextual_description: During the Islamic era, maintaining water infrastructure from earlier dynasties and building new structures were both important to sustaining water sources for agriculture and life. This aqueduct is an example. It was used to provide water to the Jericho Oasis and to support sugar cane cultivation.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/d06.contextual_description: An original field map from 'The Survey of Western Palestine' shows the water courses feeding into the Jordan Valley and River in the Jericho Oasis. It documents is an example of the documentation of water sources and pathways during the Islamic era.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/df8.contextual_description: A view of Jebel Kuruntul from the Jericho plain, with remnants of Mamluk sugar mills and aqueducts in the mid-distance. This picture provides a full view of the aqueduct and sugar mills, and illustrates the advanced structure and processing of agricultural products.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/e7e.contextual_description: An outstanding example of medieval Moroccan hydraulic engineering. The Almohads built new structures and adapted them to the semi-arid environment of Morocco. These cisterns are an example. They capture rain and floodwater using filtration and storage systems to provide water year-round for agriculture, urban life and trade.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/caf.contextual_description: One of the traditional cultivation tools, this plough was drawn by animals. A ploughman walked behind it to steer the animals and guide them in the desired direction by using a sturdy rope and verbal commands.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/917.contextual_description: The sickle is a widely-used manual agricultural tool with a curved blade. It has been typically used for harvesting grain or cutting weeds to feed livestock.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/a86.contextual_description: The sickle is a widely-used manual agricultural tool with a curved blade. It has been typically used for harvesting grain or cutting weeds to feed livestock.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/502.contextual_description: This scythe-like agricultural hand tool is traditionally used for cutting weeds and reaping crops in cultivated fields. It has an angled steel blade for maximum efficiency. Such tools demonstrate the craftsmanship of toolmaking and the efficient use of water in planting in Oman.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/c1e.contextual_description: This traditional tool for chopping and splitting wood is an indispensable tool in agriculture and construction across Islamic territories. It serves multiple functions. The steel head serves as a wedge to force wood fibres apart, and the wooden handle acts as a lever to increase force at the cutting edge.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/259.contextual_description: A soil-levelling tool used after ploughing, operated by two people using a double rope to flatten the ground and optimise the irrigation capacity of limited cultivation areas in oasis environments. It reflects a form of sustainable vernacular hydraulic know-how rooted in collective effort.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/062.contextual_description: A hand-held tool for cutting cereals during the harvest, marking the culmination of an agricultural cycle, which was all highly dependent on the careful sharing and management of water. Its worn patina, eroded over years of careful use, visibly embodies the agricultural knowledge and restrained techniques that allowed communities to thrive in arid, irrigation-dependent oasis environments.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/2ef.contextual_description: A light, versatile hoe used for weeding, shallow soil turning, and marking small water channels to maximise irrigation in oasis plots. Employed for daily micro-interventions on the soil and water flow.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/bd8.contextual_description: A wider version of the small hoe, used for maintaining the edges of irrigation plots and opening shallow channels. It illustrates the diversity and ingenuity of oasis agricultural practices that allow for the meticulous management of water and soil.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/df0.contextual_description: A sturdy tool designed for agricultural earthworks and the cleaning of irrigation canals (*seguia*). Used during seasonal and communal labour, it embodies the farmer’s dual role as both cultivator and water manager.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/ec5.contextual_description: The self-sustaining ecosystems of the oases supported food production and carried deep religious, social, and economic meanings. This image depicts veiled women in Egypt’s Sinai Peninsula grinding corn used for consumption and animal feed. The image illustrates the contributions of women in agriculture.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/994.contextual_description: Dates are one of the major crops of oases in the Arabian Peninsula, and are a source of nutrition and economic value. Date production contributed to the prominence of oases on trade routes. Not only were date palms used for their fruit, they were also used for seeds, sap, oil, syrup (molasses) and leaves.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/647.contextual_description: A tray used to harvest dates, the main product of oases, is woven from palm stems. It is an example of the use of agricultural products to create tools for planting and harvesting.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/51a.contextual_description: Dates are one of the main products of oases, used for food and traded. Dates are harvested by climbing a palm tree using this back support and rope. The climber works his way up the tree by looping the *suw’* around the trunk, leaning back against the *quffah*, and stepping upward.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/936.contextual_description: Dates are one of the main products of oases, used for food and widely traded. Dates are harvested by climbing a palm tree using this back support and rope. The climber works his way up the tree by looping the *suw’* around the trunk, leaning back against the *quffah*, and stepping upward.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/6e3.contextual_description: Date syrup, known as molasses, is a popular product in the Arabian Peninsula. It is made in the *medbasa*, a special room with grooves in the floor for collecting dibs (date syrup). The item illustrates the use of dates to produce other edible products. Several *medbasa* rooms still exist in Sharjah.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/b6a.contextual_description: The jar (known as a *dabba* in Qatar) is used to store date syrup (molasses), one of the main products of oasis agriculture. It represents a method of preserving and transporting food products.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/e0a.contextual_description: This item is an example of a unique product produced from apricots in Syria. *qamar ad din* is made from an apricot specific to the Damascus oasis, where it originated. The process involves several phases, from selection, washing and drying, to cutting into strips.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/567.contextual_description: This item is a unique product made from apricots in Syria. *Qamar ad din* comes from an apricot specific to the Damascus oasis, where it originated.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/0bc.contextual_description: This item highlights a unique product made from apricots in Syria. *Qamar ad din* comes from an apricot specific to the Damascus oasis, where it originated.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/598.contextual_description: This item highlights a unique product made from apricots in Syria. *Qamar ad din* comes from an apricot specific to the Damascus oasis, where it originated. The process involves several phases, from selection, washing and drying, to cutting into strips.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/de2.contextual_description: This drawing of a well reflects its function as a symbol of life. As the main source of water, it is the centre of life in oases. The drawing highlights the workloads and roles of men and women in daily life in rural Jordan.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/9b2.contextual_description: The well wheel is used to lift water from wells for agriculture. It is a mechanism capable of driving traditional irrigation systems. The construction of this cogged well wheel from local hardwoods such as *sidr* (Jujube), reflects a longstanding mastery of water-lifting technologies vital to agriculture in Oman’s arid environment.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/c88.contextual_description: The pulley was essential to obtaining well water. It was made in the Arabian Peninsula in the form of a wheel encircled by a rope to lift the water bucket from a well. It was a process in which animals typically were used to pull the rope that passed through the pulley.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/a34.contextual_description: Oasis agriculture was based mainly on irrigation from wells. This item was used to raise water from wells, *zājrah*, where donkeys and bullocks work side by side to pull against the weight of the water.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/269.contextual_description: The rope is an essential component of a mechanism to obtain water, used with a pulley to lift a bucket from the well.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/9c7.contextual_description: In Moroccan oases the main source of water was wells, and the *dlu* is a traditional leather bucket used to draw water for agricultural and urban purposes. The *dlu* was made of local material able to withstand repeated immersion in water.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/836.contextual_description: The robust engineering of this *ad-dalū* reflects a long-standing tradition of irrigation technologies essential for survival in Oman’s arid landscape. The leather bag is designed to lift water from deep wells and reservoirs by relying on the power of draft animals walking along an inclined path. As the animals ascend, the *dalū* is lowered into the source and filled with water. The animals descend with the filled bag.

71c38013-b2d8-5de1-a4d0-715042c6db6c/16c.contextual_description: Wells represent the major source of water in oases. Inhabitants draw water from deep wells using various means. The pulley and rope in the Arabian Peninsula are used to draw water for drinking and watering animals. This is one type of leather bucket.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b/951.contextual_description: Villages are typical social and economic structures in the River Nile Valley, where a majority of agricultural activities are based. Inhabitants of the village are mainly engaged in agriculture, animal raising and trading. This is a scene depicting the lives of Egyptians in a local village on the Nile. It shows a market stall with men and women engaging in commerce in a natural setting.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b/057.contextual_description: Agricultural wonders in the Ottoman Empire were not limited to agricultural products; gardens were also important. This is the inner garden at the Yildiz Palace, in Beşiktaş, Türkiye, where winter gardens and greenhouses were built. Some were heated for growing special plants.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b/c2b.contextual_description: Syria’s historic water distribution systems helped transform a dry region into a thriving centre of civilisation. In Damascus, Roman canals, Ayyubid engineering and channels fed by the Barada River supplied homes, mosques, hammams and schools with running water. The tali system allocated water to each neighbourhood in fixed shares, as overseen by an official to ensure fairness. Similar systems shaped Aleppo and Hama, where canals and norias supported urban life and irrigation.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b/82a.contextual_description: Noria Jisriyya and Ma’muriyya in Hama are among the most significant waterwheels on the Orontes River. The Jisriyya once irrigated the orchards of Bustan al-Shahiqa, and part of its aqueduct is still standing. The Ma’muriyya is the largest after the Muhammadiyya. This noria carries a rare Ottoman inscription recording its renovation by an Ottoman governor in AH 857 / AH 1453, demonstrating the empire’s attention to water resources and agriculture.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b/ccf.contextual_description:
A wooden waterwheel known locally as naoor (plural: nawa'ir), traditionally used to lift water for irrigation along the upper Euphrates, from Syria into Anbar governorate in western Iraq.  
Most nawa'ir were ranging from 8-12 metres in diameter and were constructed from mulberry wood (known for durability), cut to size and connected with wooden pegs hammered into place. As the river current caused the wheels to rotate, the jars would raise water from the river and pour it into an aqueduct at the top of the stone platform, which fed into irrigation channels leading to nearby farms.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b/3d1.contextual_description: This map illustrates water networks around Lebanon under Ottoman administration, reflecting state-led efforts to organise, control, and expand water supply systems. It highlights how hydraulic infrastructure supported agriculture, urban life, and regional connectivity, and reveals the role of imperial governance in managing water as a strategic and economic resource.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b/f32.contextual_description: Wellheads were used to facilitate access to a well’s water and to protect wells from being polluted. This type of wellhead is distinctive to southern Spain when the region was under Muslim domination. Aside from its functionality and usefulness, it displays artistic embellishments in its inscription and attractive decorations.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b/1df.contextual_description: Wellheads were used to facilitate access to the well’s water and to protect it from being polluted. This wellhead from Türkiye is terracotta, and has decorations in the form of chain-like incised lines with circular geometrical shapes in between.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b/adb.contextual_description: This item shows an essential agricultural tool. It is used for dividing fields into manageable plots and creating water channels in the local *falaj* system. It is part of an agricultural system, and is evidence of cooperation among workers.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b/a55.contextual_description: The development of irrigation and hydraulic systems in al-Andalus enabled the introduction of new plant species, expanded arable land and diversified the diet. It changed working methods and the agricultural cycle. Waterwheels spread throughout the Iberian Peninsula. The waterwheel buckets, attached by ropes at the mouth and midway along their cylindrical body, represented small technical advances. The oldest ones, with an annular or pointed bottom, gradually gave way to others with a perforated bottom that prevented tilting and breaking, or the backward movement of the wheel.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b/c47.contextual_description: Almond planting was first introduced in the southern region of Portugal. There is a legend that tells how almond trees came to be part of the landscape. An Arab prince, married to a Christian from the north, noticed that his wife lived in a permanent state of melancholy. So, one day he asked her for the reason for this enduring mood. She told him that she missed the snow, frequent in the north of the peninsula. The prince then ordered the planting of almond trees, whose blossoming at the end of winter would create the illusion of fields covered with snow.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b/85f.contextual_description: Almond trees were not only a source of edible fruit and nuts, but extracts from the tree have been used for dyeing clothes and for medicinal purposes. This image shows the leaves of an almond tree.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b/0d4.contextual_description: Coffee has its roots in Yemen as a drink of the Sufi religious order, and with the expansion of Islam, coffee spread from the Arabian Peninsula to the whole world, becoming very popular. This item illustrates how new crops were introduced in different areas through the expansion of the Islamic Empire.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b/5f4.contextual_description: *Haal* (cardamom) is a plant that has a distinctive smell and is widely used to flavour coffee.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b/401.contextual_description: Cotton is one of the important products in plains- and river-based agriculture that expanded to several countries during the Islamic era. Palestine became a viable cotton producer in the AH 13th / AD 19th century, supplying European countries, but the industry declined, as it was based on cultivation and not processing. This engraving shows a Palestinian woman in Wady et Tuffah using the traditional spinning wheel for cotton. It also highlights the role of agriculture in trade in the region.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b/048.contextual_description: Quality cotton was produced in several countries of the Islamic civilisation. A large volume of the produce was exported to Europe as raw, unprocessed material. Egypt was one of the countries that had remarkable cotton production and export trade.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b/92a.contextual_description: This basket is used by fishermen to store fish. It is an indigenous basket made using local materials such as bamboo and jute. It filters out the water and leaves only the fish.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b/550.contextual_description: This rectangular trap is made of fine bamboo. It is used to catch small fish.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b/696.contextual_description: A hat made of palm leaves and bamboo for protection from rain and sun.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b/ba6.contextual_description: A traditional object made of coconut shell and used for smoking that demonstrates the use of agricultural materials in the production of daily-use objects.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b/f9d.contextual_description: This item illustrates the usage of agricultural products for other functions. Gourds can be harvested young for consumption as a vegetable, if grown as containers or utensils they are left to grow for longer and harvested when mature. After harvesting, they are dried for several months until the outer shell becomes hard. The dried gourds are usually cut at the top to make an opening through which the seeds are removed and contents added for storage.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b/5e3.contextual_description: This item illustrates the usage of agricultural products for other functions. Gourds can be harvested young for consumption as a vegetable, if grown as containers or utensils they are left to grow for longer and harvested when mature. After harvesting, they are dried for several months until the outer shell becomes hard. The dried gourds are usually cut at the top to make an opening through which the seeds are removed and contents added for storage.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b/c96.contextual_description: This is a tool used to produce flour from grains like wheat and barley. *Al rahaa* (millstone) is used to grind grains that are fed between two stones through a central hole. It is an example of an agricultural tool used in the region.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b/5f6.contextual_description: These mills reflected the development of hydraulic infrastructure and rationed use of water. They were often connected to other hydraulic structures. Water mills harnessed the power of flowing water to grind cereals such as wheat, barley, and corn for food and trade.

4ba33798-b360-52eb-90f1-614e0e8be75b/888.contextual_description: Olive trees were planted in several countries across the Islamic Empire. They were used for food and for the production of related products, including oil. Tunisia is one of the countries renowned for olive oil production.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0/272.contextual_description: These dams reflect early Islamic innovation in managing scarce water for farming. Al-Qanatir refers to two Umayyad-period stone dams south of al-Qastal that collected and stored rainwater for agriculture. Their name echoes qanat, the ingenious Islamic water systems. Built across wadis, the dams reach 187m in length and 9m in height, and have stone walls with insulating plaster, spillways and sluices to regulate water. Nearby remnants point to a small guardhouse.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0/b7c.contextual_description: This aqueduct was used to transport and supply water from the Nile to the Citadel of Salah al-Din in Cairo. It was first planned in the Ayyubid period. Water was lifted by wheels to a canal on top of the city wall, and was carried to the citadel for drinking and irrigating nearby fields. In AH 712 / AD 1312, Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad expanded the system with a new tower, four waterwheels, and a long arcade of arches leading to the citadel. Later Mamluk rulers repaired and improved it. The surviving 3km length is a remnant of one of the finest aqueducts in the Islamic world.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0/a5f.contextual_description: Birkat al-Hajj has a significant importance as a water reservoir, and reflects the efforts to build such reservoirs by lining them with basalt. The water was used for drinking and agriculture. The reservoir was described by Ibn Battuta as a key stop for pilgrims on the route to Mecca.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0/2ba.contextual_description: The cistern was the Amman Citadel’s main water source for all purposes. This cistern demonstrates how rainwater was captured and stored here, echoing broader water-management strategies and showing how such systems sustained life and agriculture in dry regions.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0/ff7.contextual_description: The Pools of Solomon are three large stepped reservoirs that collect spring and rainwater south of Jerusalem. Linked by channels so that each fed the next, together they held more than 250,000 cubic metres of water. An aqueduct over 70km long carried water from the pools to Jerusalem, using the natural slope of the land. This system supplied the city with water for drinking, domestic needs and ablutions. The Ottomans later protected the route, even building a small fort near the upper pool.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0/8c0.contextual_description: The Pools of Solomon are three large stepped reservoirs that collect spring and rainwater south of Jerusalem. Linked by channels so that each fed the next, together they held more than 250,000 cubic metres of water. An aqueduct over 70km long carried water from the pools to Jerusalem, using the natural slope of the land. This system supplied the city with water for drinking, domestic needs and ablutions. The Ottomans later protected the route, even building a small fort near the upper pool.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0/9fe.contextual_description: The great Beni-Isguen Dam sits upstream of the Qsar in the N’tissa Wadi, Algeria. Built to manage seasonal floods and secure water for agriculture, it has two key parts: the spillway, along which are set stones for measuring the water level and to provide an alert in case of dangerous floods, and the reservoir in contact with ground water via two wheels.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0/53d.contextual_description: The Aghlabid reservoirs, once part of a system of about fifteen cisterns outside Kairouan, Tunisia, are among the most remarkable hydraulic works of the Islamic world. Fed by rainwater, local tributaries and later by an aqueduct from the Shreshira springs, they secured the city’s water supply. The surviving small and large reservoirs, built with rubble and waterproof plaster, used alternating buttresses for strength. Water settled in the small basin before flowing into the vast circular pool that stored water for daily life.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0/98f.contextual_description: This watercolour documents one of the natural springs supplying the reservoir complex known as Solomon’s Pools at Artas. It depicts the vaulted Spring House, where water from ‘Ain Farujeh is collected and channelled into the Lower Pool, the largest of three reservoirs. Integrated into the eastern dam wall, this structure illustrates the careful control of water flow within the system.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0/039.contextual_description: *Foggaras* are ingenious Saharan water systems that bring underground water to the surface through a series of horizontal wells on gentle slopes, allowing irrigation of palm groves and gardens. Tunnels follow aquifers with precise gradients, and water is pooled and distributed via channels and ponds according to communal needs. Found across the Aurora and Touat oases, *foggaras* demonstrate early, large-scale engineering and cooperative management of scarce desert water for agriculture and survival.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0/06a.contextual_description: The nilometer is one of Egypt’s most important hydraulic structures and is unique in the Islamic world. It measured the water level of the Nile, which determined both irrigation and agricultural taxes. Built as a deep stone well with three levels and a central marble pillar marked with measurements, it received water through underground tunnels. It includes early pointed arches, a spiral staircase and some of Egypt’s oldest dated Arabic inscriptions. Restored many times, it reflects the long history of Nile management.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0/706.contextual_description: The bridge spans the Medjerda River about two kilometres downstream from Tbourba. Commissioned by the Ottoman government, the Bridge-Dam of al-Battan was constructed around AH 1101 / AD 1690 under Bey Mohamed, son of Murad II. This impressive hydraulic structure combines engineering with architectural grace: sixteen arches rise above a solid inverted vault base that anchors the entire dam. The dam was an important instrument in regulating water flow to ensure availability year-round, while providing transport across the river.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0/50f.contextual_description: This inscription comes from the nilometer on the island of al-Rauda in Cairo, a structure built in AD 861 to measure the annual rise of the Nile. Quranic inscriptions within the monument reflect the spiritual dimension attached to water as a divine provision.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0/0f1.contextual_description: The Fuad Agriculture Museum, opened in the 1930s during the reign of King Faruq, was the first museum of its kind in the Middle East and the Arab world. It presents extensive collections on agricultural life, rural environments and the plants and animals that shaped daily work and food production. The museum reflects modern Egypt’s effort to document and preserve the heritage of farming, a foundation of life along the Nile.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0/47e.contextual_description: Norias were an important mechanism to lift water from rivers for wider distribution for irrigation and urban life. Hama’s norias, built with wooden wheels and stone aqueducts, could lift around 50 litres of water per second to irrigate vast orchards and supply city quarters. It is the defining symbol of Hama on the River Orontes.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0/6cf.contextual_description: Developed to sustain agriculture and settlement in arid landscapes, the *aflaj* of Oman form a highly refined system of managing scarce groundwater resources. Drawing on deep aquifers, water is carefully guided through gently sloping subterranean channels before emerging into open canals that irrigate fields and supply villages.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0/780.contextual_description: Developed to sustain agriculture and settlement in arid landscapes, the *aflaj* of Oman form a highly refined system of managing scarce groundwater resources. Drawing on deep aquifers, water is carefully guided through gently sloping subterranean channels before emerging into open canals that irrigate fields and supply villages.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0/826.contextual_description: The noria is an ancient waterwheel used to lift and distribute river water by harnessing the force of a running stream. In Hama, on the River Orontes, nawa’ir became central to urban life from antiquity through the Islamic periods, with major expansion and restoration under the Seljuqs, Zangids, Ayyubids, Mamluks, and Ottomans. Combining wooden wheels with stone aqueducts and dams, these structures supplied water for irrigation, mosques, and households, shaping both the landscape and identity of the city.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0/e7f.contextual_description: Sahrij Swani, the great Basin of Norias in Meknes, was created by Sultan Mulay Isma’il as both an ornamental lake and a secure water reserve for the palaces, mosques, baths, homes and orchards of the kasbah. It is a demonstration of the growing attention to ensuring availability of water for all purposes.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0/cc3.contextual_description: This stone capital belonged to a water reservoir at the Umayyad palace of al-Muwaqqar, commissioned by Caliph Yazid II (AH 101-105 / AD 720–724). Decorated with acanthus leaves and paired volutes, it bears inscriptions in Arabic that record the reservoir’s construction and measurements in cubits, serving as a water gauge. The highest level, 15 cubits, is marked on the capital itself. Another inscription invokes blessings on Muhammad. The piece demonstrates early Islamic engineering and the integration of art and hydraulic function.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0/3e0.contextual_description: The *kırkçeşme* water supply system, built under Sultan Süleyman and designed by Mimar Sinan in the 16th century, collected water from springs 25km northwest of Istanbul, and conveyed it through 55km of covered galleries; 33 aqueducts, such as Mağlova and Uzunkemer, carried water across valleys. The system supplied hundreds of fountains, mosques, and public buildings, ensuring running water for the growing population. Parts of it remain functional over 400 years later.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0/70e.contextual_description: The Zaghwan Aqueduct reflects Tunisia’s long effort to secure reliable water for its cities. In AH 1275 / AD 1859, Mohamed Bey commissioned engineer Pierre Colin to restore the abandoned Roman aqueduct from Zaghwan to Carthage, along with its Hafsid diversion to Tunis. Completed in AH 1278 / AD 1862, the project refurbished nearly 90km of canal and added 41km of metal piping, ensuring water for Tunis and the Bey’s residences. Its striking arches remain visible today.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0/8ee.contextual_description: Built in AH 1319 / AD 1902 under Sultan Abdülhamid II, the Cendere Hamidian Water Pump Station showcases the technological advances that reshaped AD 13th / AD 19th–century travel and communication. Using steam powered pumps, the station pumped water arriving through 20 pipes from Kağıthane, and supplied Balmumcu and Beşiktaş toward Tophane. Its engineering, machinery and architecture make it a rare industrial monument of the late Ottoman period.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0/854.contextual_description: Built in the AH 13th / AD 19th century, the water elevation towers of Tameslought supported agricultural life in a semi-arid landscape southeast of Marrakech. Designed to irrigate extensive olive groves, these towers used pressurisation and inverted siphon principles to lift water from lower sources to higher fields without animal or human labour. Constructed from local materials, they enabled efficient irrigation, strengthened olive oil production and encouraged collective water management, reflecting both technical ingenuity and strong communal organisation.

6516014a-c6c1-5ceb-97a3-d695462efde0/40a.contextual_description: Khettaras are gravity-fed underground water systems adapted from the Persian qanat and introduced to Morocco during the Islamic period. Since the AH 7th / AD 11th century, particularly under the Almoravids, they became essential in regions such as the Haouz near Marrakech, later spreading to southern oasis zones. By channelling groundwater through gently sloping tunnels and vertical shafts, khettaras supplied farms and settlements without mechanical energy. Beyond their hydraulic ingenuity, they structured agricultural production, settlement patterns, and communal water law, shaping social and political life in Morocco’s arid landscapes.

eb0a0f58-72d0-5c98-a5dc-283759eac032/adf.contextual_description: This folio comes from a Persian translation of 'The Wonders of Creation and the Oddities of Existence' by Zakaria ibn Muhammad al-Qazwini. It is a celebrated AH 7th / AD 13th century cosmography that brought together geography, astronomy, astrology, and natural history. Blending scientific observation with marvels and symbolic knowledge, the work reflects medieval understandings of the natural world. The folio is richly decorated on both sides with miniatures of fruit-bearing trees, evoking abundance, order, and the harmony of creation as conceived in the Islamic intellectual tradition.

eb0a0f58-72d0-5c98-a5dc-283759eac032/43d.contextual_description: This illustration depicts the Delta Barrage, a dam constructed in the early AH 13th / AD 19th century under Muhammad Ali Pasha and designed by the French engineer Mougelle to regulate the Nile’s flow throughout the year. Spanning the Damietta and Rosetta branches, this dam controlled water levels for irrigation, and also served a defensive role in protecting Cairo and Upper Egypt. Structural weaknesses required major improvements beginning in AH 1300 / AD 1883, under Sir Colin Scott Moncrieff. The Delta Barrage reflects Egypt's long tradition of large-scale hydraulic works essential to agriculture and state power.

eb0a0f58-72d0-5c98-a5dc-283759eac032/b67.contextual_description: This illustrated page comes from *Voyage d’Egypte et de Nubie*, compiled by the Danish naval officer Fréderic-Louis Norden during his mission to document Egypt’s monuments in the early AH 12th / AD 18th century. Published after his death, and later expanded with scientific commentary by the orientalist Louis Langles, the work reflects the period’s growing European fascination with Egypt. Here, the focus is on traditional hydraulic machines, highlighting water-lifting technologies as objects of study and knowledge within agricultural science and the scholarly observation of water management.

eb0a0f58-72d0-5c98-a5dc-283759eac032/ef4.contextual_description: Dioscorides, born in the 1st century AD in Anazarbus, authored *De Materia Medica*, a foundational treatise on plants, minerals, and natural substances that shaped medical and agricultural knowledge for over a millennium. Translated into Syriac and later into Arabic in AH 3th / AD 9th century Baghdad by Istafan bin Basil and Hunayn ibn Ishaq at the Abbasid court, the work entered the scholarly canon of the Islamic world. Continuously revised and illustrated, it informed pharmacology, botany, and water management. A famous Arabic version, known as '*Khawass al-Ashjar*' circulated in the AH 7th / AD 13th century. The treatise reflects the integration of classical science into Islamic traditions of knowledge.

eb0a0f58-72d0-5c98-a5dc-283759eac032/cfb.contextual_description: The *acte habus*, or *waqf* deed, documents the charitable endowment of water rights in Islamic Morocco, recording how a designated share of water was permanently assigned to a mosque, madrasa, or public fountain. Rooted in the belief that water is a divine trust, such deeds linked irrigation and domestic supply to religious merit and social responsibility. Beyond their legal role, these documents reveal how water management was embedded in moral values, ensuring continuity of access, community welfare, and the sacred stewardship of a vital resource.

eb0a0f58-72d0-5c98-a5dc-283759eac032/35b.contextual_description: This manuscript contains a *fatwa*, or Islamic legal/religious opinion, addressing the management and equitable distribution of water in Moroccan society. Issued by a jurist in AH 14th / AD mid-20th century Marrakech, it shows how Islamic law governed irrigation rights, resolved disputes between users, and framed water as a sacred trust requiring fairness. The document reflects the enduring role of religious scholarship in shaping ethical water stewardship, complementing customary practices and reinforcing water as a collective right entrusted by God.

eb0a0f58-72d0-5c98-a5dc-283759eac032/54b.contextual_description: Mastery of water distribution was fundamental to the cultivation of gardens and the sustaining of urban life, making this waterway an expression of agricultural knowledge in practice. Fed by the Aupah (Kirazlı) and Çınar springs, the highest-capacity branches of the Halkalı system, the Süleymaniye waterway supplied the entire Süleymaniye complex, including its *imaret* (soup kitchen), *maristan* (hospital), *maktab* (school), public fountains, and some 80 additional points across Istanbul. The map records how water was conveyed into the city and allocated among key quarters, revealing the technical expertise and planning that linked hydraulic engineering, garden cultivation, and imperial welfare.

eb0a0f58-72d0-5c98-a5dc-283759eac032/b58.contextual_description:
An original plan from 'The Survey of Western Palestine' showing aqueducts bringing water from wadies Fara, Kelt and Nuwayimeh into the Jericho Oasis. These aqueducts date from the Hellenistic era to the Umayyad-period Khirbet al Mafjar, a huge agricultural estate and palace, and the Mamluk-period sugar mill, Tawaheen es Sukkar.  
  
The aqueduct was constructed in the Hellenistic era and was used and added to for centuries well into the Islamic era.

eb0a0f58-72d0-5c98-a5dc-283759eac032/b5d.contextual_description: By regulating access to water essential for irrigation and rural livelihoods, this imperial Ottoman decree (*ferman*), issued during the reign of Abdülmecid, highlights the legal frameworks that sustained agricultural production. Addressing water distribution to the villages of the Eşeközü hamlet in the Kayseri district, it demonstrates how state authority, agricultural needs, and hydraulic knowledge were closely linked in the governance of cultivated landscapes.

eb0a0f58-72d0-5c98-a5dc-283759eac032/5fc.contextual_description: By documenting the techniques that enabled irrigation and the cultivation of land, this technical manuscript reflects the close relationship between agriculture and scholarly knowledge in the Ottoman world. Describing water channels, wells, and pumping systems, it demonstrates how agricultural productivity depended on carefully studied hydraulic engineering. Such manuscripts transmit practical knowledge developed by engineers and scholars, showing that farming was supported not only by labour and experience but also by written science and technical expertise.

eb0a0f58-72d0-5c98-a5dc-283759eac032/266.contextual_description: This manuscript illustrates the intersection of scholarship and hydraulic engineering in medieval Islamic societies. In the early AH 7th / AD 13th century, Isma’il ibn al-Razzaz al-Jazari wrote *Kitab fi ma’rifat al-hiyal al-handasiyya* ('The Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices'), detailing elaborate machines in courtly settings in eastern Anatolia. This AH 755 / AD 1354 Mamluk copy, produced by Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Izmiri, preserves text and illustrations, showing the advanced understanding of mechanics and water management applied to gardens and decorative devices.

eb0a0f58-72d0-5c98-a5dc-283759eac032/f29.contextual_description: Al-Jazari’s book demonstrates the rich intellectual engagement with mechanical inventions in the medieval Islamic world. This page depicts a series of intricate devices, highlighting the combination of creativity and functional design. The illustrations show how engineers conceptualised and communicated complex mechanisms, reflecting a tradition of practical experimentation and knowledge-sharing that extended beyond al-Jazari’s own workshop to inform subsequent generations of scholars and artisans.

eb0a0f58-72d0-5c98-a5dc-283759eac032/216.contextual_description: Water-intensive farming and settlement life relied on devices that could lift water from rivers, wells, or channels to higher ground. This depiction highlights the use of animal power, here a donkey, to operate a mechanical system that transfers water efficiently, translating theoretical understanding into practical action. Such mechanisms demonstrate how engineering knowledge was embedded in daily agricultural practice, responding to local environments and labour resources while ensuring a steady water supply for fields and communities.

eb0a0f58-72d0-5c98-a5dc-283759eac032/8f4.contextual_description: This folio depicts a sophisticated water clock in which flowing water activates a system of wheels and moving figures to mark the passage of time. By transforming hydraulic motion into visual and acoustic signals, the device demonstrates how water was used as a medium for precise measurement. Its carefully coordinated elements reflect an advanced understanding of flow, control, and mechanical balance, showing how scholarly knowledge translated natural forces into regulated systems that structured daily life.

aff608af-f2c7-54b7-8325-794e1d8d4ba1/84c.contextual_description: The Haram al-Sharif ('Noble Sanctuary') in Jerusalem is the third most important site in Islam after Mecca and Medina. It includes Qubbat al-Sakhra (Dome of the Rock) and al-Aqsa Mosque, which were built in AH 72 / AD 692 and AH 86 / AD 705 respectively. The Haram al-Sharif is where the Prophet Muhammad set out on his midnight journey from Mecca to Jerusalem (*isra*) and from where he ascended to the heavens (*miraj*).

aff608af-f2c7-54b7-8325-794e1d8d4ba1/a6b.contextual_description: A freestanding sabil commissioned by the Mamluk Sultan al-Ashraf Qaytbay (r. AH 872–901 / AD 1468–96) continues to provide visitors to the Haram al-Sharif with fresh water. Built in the late AH 9th / AD 15th century, it was executed in a style reminiscent of Mamluk Cairo, distinguished by alternating courses of red and yellow stone (*ablaq*) and an elaborately carved dome.

aff608af-f2c7-54b7-8325-794e1d8d4ba1/1af.contextual_description: Captured in the early AH 14 / AD 20th century, this photograph shows officials taking part in one of the ceremonies related to the opening of a newly restored aqueduct outside al-Aqsa Mosque in the *Haram al-Sharif*.

aff608af-f2c7-54b7-8325-794e1d8d4ba1/54b.contextual_description:
Designed to supply water to the entire Süleymaniye Complex in Istanbul— including the ancillary structures that provided religious and cultural services — the Süleymaniye waterway also extended to districts inhabited by courtiers and dignitaries.  
  
This AH 12th / AD 18th century map is significant because it not only informs the ways in which water was brought to Istanbul, but illustrates the social topography of a major city linking Europe and Asia.

aff608af-f2c7-54b7-8325-794e1d8d4ba1/6b7.contextual_description:
The Süleymaniye was commissioned by Sultan Süleyman the Magnificent (r. AH 926–74 / AD 1520–66) and designed by the imperial architect Mimar Sinan. Like other Ottoman imperial foundations in Türkiye, the mosque is part of a larger *külliye* that included four *madrasa*s, *imaret*, *maristan*, *maktab*, public fountains and the final resting place of Süleyman and his wife Hurrem Sultan (Roxelana).  
  
The largest Ottoman-period complex in Istanbul, it is considered a masterpiece of Ottoman architecture and one of Sinan’s greatest works.

aff608af-f2c7-54b7-8325-794e1d8d4ba1/3d8.contextual_description: The centrepiece of the Süleymaniye Complex is the courtyard mosque surrounded by an enclosure wall. The two sets of buildings to the right and left of the mosque are the four *madrasa*s; the small domed building on the lower right is the bathhouse; and the hospital, hospice, and guesthouse are located at the top of the map. All units would have been served by water carried by the Süleymaniye waterway.

aff608af-f2c7-54b7-8325-794e1d8d4ba1/3e0.contextual_description: Like the Süleymaniye Complex, the Kırkçeşme water-supply system was commissioned by Sultan Süleyman and designed by Mimar Sinan around AH 971 / AD 1564. It consists of 33 aqueducts that addressed Istanbul’s water shortage, and originally served over 300 fountains, later extended to 580, across the city.

aff608af-f2c7-54b7-8325-794e1d8d4ba1/997.contextual_description: Abd al-Rahman Katkhuda (d. AH 1190 / AD 1776) was a leader of the janissaries in Egypt and a significant patron of architecture in Cairo. Among the many buildings bearing his name is this two-story institution that combined two distinct acts of charity: on the lower level is the *sabil* or public drinking fountain; which is surmounted by an elementary school (*kuttab*) that provided instruction in reading, writing, Arabic grammar, and Quran recitation. *Sabil-kuttab*s were most common in Cairo during the Mamluk and subsequent Ottoman periods.

aff608af-f2c7-54b7-8325-794e1d8d4ba1/2c3.contextual_description: Built by Husayn Pasha, a high-ranking officer, this public drinking fountain manifests the Islamic tradition of charitable water endowments. Inscribed with the phrase "Everything lives through water," it provided refreshment for the community while proclaiming the patron’s piety and generosity. Originally located outside Bab al-Djazira, the fountain was later relocated several times, but continued to symbolise the civic and spiritual importance of water in Ottoman Algiers.

aff608af-f2c7-54b7-8325-794e1d8d4ba1/cdd.contextual_description: A landmark of Istanbul’s Tulip Era, this monumental fountain features four *sabil*s, one at each corner of the building. Commissioned by the Ottoman Sultan Ahmed III (r. AH 1115–42 / AD 1703–30), the rich marble decoration and baroque floral motifs paired with Ottoman inscriptions represent the trend of combining imperial patronage with Western influences introduced into the 18th-century Ottoman domain.

aff608af-f2c7-54b7-8325-794e1d8d4ba1/be9.contextual_description:
Very different from the previous examples of Ottoman-period public drinking fountains, this one, in the shape of a bench, was built by the governor of Damascus in honour of Sultan Süleyman the Magnificent in AH 971 / AD 1564. It was originally installed in his mosque in Damascus, which was demolished in AH 1348 / AD 1930, after which the fountain was salvaged and moved to the National Museum.  
  
Carved from fine marble and richly decorated with *diwani* calligraphy (popular at the time), geometric mosaics, and mother-of-pearl inlay, it demonstrates the importance of charitable water provisions and elite patronage in the urban and religious life of AH 10th / AD 16th-century Damascus.

6b701948-1e27-542e-a3fb-9f27270569b8/fa9.contextual_description: Named "*Badiʿ*", or "the incomparable", this palace was famed for its courtyard pools, fountains, and surrounding gardens. Though much of the palace is now in ruins, its vast basins are a reminder of how water and greenery created an earthly vision of paradise, where water was employed for luxury and spectacle.

6b701948-1e27-542e-a3fb-9f27270569b8/9ef.contextual_description: Founded by Fatima al-Fihriya, the daughter of a wealthy merchant from Kairouan, the Qarawiyyin Mosque in Fez incorporated pools and hydraulic channels to supply water for ablution and refreshment. Water from local wells was directed into the courtyard, where its presence enhanced both function and aesthetics. Drawing on the Andalusi and Maghribi tradition of integrating water into architecture, these pools echoed the Quranic image of gardens beneath which rivers flow (al-Taqwah: 72 and 89), transforming the mosque into a place of prayer and an image of paradise.

6b701948-1e27-542e-a3fb-9f27270569b8/1ab.contextual_description: Inlaid with polychrome marble, this small fountain was typical of Ottoman public and garden spaces. Its flowing water created soothing soundscapes, sometimes even masking conversations in official meetings. Beyond utility, such fountains contributed to the atmosphere of privacy, comfort, and contemplation within gardens and courtyards.

6b701948-1e27-542e-a3fb-9f27270569b8/e73.contextual_description: Discovered at the palace of Dar al-Bahr in Qalʿat Bani Hammad, this marble fountain basin once formed part of a larger water system. Its functional design included an outlet for water pipes, highlighting its dual role as a utilitarian and decorative feature in a palace context.

6b701948-1e27-542e-a3fb-9f27270569b8/c8a.contextual_description: Richly decorated with Italian marble, ceramic tiles, and stucco, Dar Ibn ‘Abd Allah is organised around a courtyard centered on a fountain with three tiered basins. The architecture integrates water into the domestic setting, offering refreshment and tranquillity.

6b701948-1e27-542e-a3fb-9f27270569b8/d53.contextual_description: This cast-bronze vessel shaped like a ram once served as a fountainhead or aquamanile in a palace or large home. Water was channelled through the body and poured from the open mouth. Such animal-shaped vessels were popular across the Islamic world, blending symbolic imagery, craftsmanship, and the practical needs of domestic life.

6b701948-1e27-542e-a3fb-9f27270569b8/d9d.contextual_description: This hollow cast-bronze lion once served as part of a fountain, with water spouting from its open mouth. Its abstract, stylised form, spiral patterns, and inscription link it to Fatimid Egypt, where courtly taste encouraged figural sculpture. Likely part of a larger ensemble of animal figures, it demonstrates how water features combined utility, artistic experimentation, and symbolic imagery.

6b701948-1e27-542e-a3fb-9f27270569b8/94b.contextual_description: Although its provenance is unknown, the discovery of this gilded hind in the Cordoba region suggests that it once decorated an Andalusi palace fountain. Yet, it is chronologically connected to the ram and lion in this same series. Hollow, it channelled water through the body, animating palace gardens with sound and motion.

6b701948-1e27-542e-a3fb-9f27270569b8/423.contextual_description:
A longstanding misconception regarding this object is that it was an ablutions basin. However, this ​​trough-shaped basin has an inscription that clearly states it was made for al-Madinat al-Zahira, a palace-city east of Cordoba, not to be confused with the more popular caliphal foundation of Madinat al-Zahra, west of Cordoba, which it imitated. The former was built by al-Mansur, the vizier of caliph Hisham II, from AH 368/AD 978–979 to AH 370 / AD 980–981, and was subsequently sacked and destroyed in AH 399 / AD 1009.  
  
According to recent scholarship, this basin is the only definitively identifiable physical object to survive from al-Mansur’s palace-city.

6b701948-1e27-542e-a3fb-9f27270569b8/f32.contextual_description: Designed to crown and protect a well, this ceramic wellhead from al-Andalus formed a permanent architectural feature within domestic or courtyard spaces. Bands of gazelles, birds, and a Kufic inscription decorate its surface, highlighting the technical skill of Andalusi potters and the care invested in objects linked to water use.

6b701948-1e27-542e-a3fb-9f27270569b8/57c.contextual_description: During the Almohad period of the Maghreb and al-Andalus, this type of well cover was widely used. It was built to protect wells in domestic courtyards.

c313de84-08f6-5017-93b2-06aba8eeb41a/737.contextual_description: Beyond its practical use in serving liquids, this turquoise-glazed ewer belongs to the Seljuq golden age of Islamic ceramics (AH 6th to early 7th centuries / AD 12th to early 13th centuries). Its refined decoration highlights the era’s technical experimentation with new materials and artistic sophistication. Such ewers were common in domestic and courtly contexts, blending daily function with aesthetic refinement.

c313de84-08f6-5017-93b2-06aba8eeb41a/65d.contextual_description: Earthenware pitches such as this example found at an archaeological site in Qatar were used for storing and pouring water in domestic settings. Its surface is decorated with embossed Arabic inscriptions and raised dot motifs, combining everyday function with ornamental detail characteristic of Seljuq ceramic production.

c313de84-08f6-5017-93b2-06aba8eeb41a/fc0.contextual_description: This incised earthenware strainer was built into a jug designed to filter water and keep it clean. Decorated with a gazelle motif against a filigree background, it exemplifies how even simple utilitarian objects were transformed into finely-crafted works.

c313de84-08f6-5017-93b2-06aba8eeb41a/d5b.contextual_description: Part of the celebrated group signed by the craftsman Ahmad, this bronze ewer features a pear-shaped body, a tall faceted neck, and a beak-shaped spout. Found in the Ferghana Valley of Central Asia, it demonstrates the sophistication of Seljuq metalwork, combining refined decoration with practical use. It would have been used in an elite household for pouring water during ablutions or meals, and embodies the artistic innovation of the Seljuq period.

c313de84-08f6-5017-93b2-06aba8eeb41a/f4e.contextual_description: This is one of the most famous surviving examples of metalwork from Mosul in Iraq. The medallions covering its body depict courtly life: princes, noblewomen, musicians, hunters, and even scenes from the Persian epic *Shahnama*. Signed by Shuja ibn Mana ʿal-Mawsili, the ewer is an excellent example of the prestige of Mosul’s workshops, which produced vessels for rulers and courts across the Islamic world. After the Mongol invasion of Iraq in AH 656 / AD 1258, craftsmen from Mosul emigrated to Mamluk Egypt and Syria, greatly influencing contemporaneous metalwork in the eastern Mediterranean.

c313de84-08f6-5017-93b2-06aba8eeb41a/00f.contextual_description: Made for Amir Tabtaq, governor of Qus under Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad, this large copper ewer is adorned with inscriptions, silver inlay, the blazon of the cupbearer, vegetal motifs, and paired birds. It exemplifies the refined workmanship of Mamluk metalworkers. Used for handwashing, bathing, or ritual ablution, it functioned as both a utilitarian tool and a mark of elite status.

c313de84-08f6-5017-93b2-06aba8eeb41a/083.contextual_description:
Made of stiff auburn leather, this conical water flask is embroidered with delicate gold and silver tendrils and rosettes.  
It is richly decorated with embroidery and ornament, suggesting it was not just a rugged portable container but also a valued household or ceremonial item. Such decorated leather flasks were used for carrying water, combining functionality with refined ornament.

c313de84-08f6-5017-93b2-06aba8eeb41a/d0f.contextual_description: Highly-crafted and inlaid metalware intended to hold water was not limited to ewers. Here is an example of an inlaid brass bowl with decoration and scenes alluding to its use. Inside are fish, creating an illusion of water, an effect that would have been intensified when the bowl was filled with water.

6df2d667-393f-56fd-ac89-764ecf509141/b7c.contextual_description: This Mamluk-period aqueduct was constructed to carry water from the Nile to the Citadel of Salah al-Din, the seat of power, ensuring a reliable supply for drinking, irrigation, and the needs of the city’s growing population. Combining waterwheels, canals, and monumental arches, it stands as a major example of large-scale hydraulic engineering and urban infrastructure in medieval Cairo.

6df2d667-393f-56fd-ac89-764ecf509141/47e.contextual_description: The great wooden waterwheels of Hama, set along the Orontes River, lifted water into stone aqueducts for urban use and irrigation. Some reached over 20 metres in diameter, and could raise up to 50 litres of water per second. Their rhythmic sound and monumental scale made them practical and symbolic landmarks of the city.

6df2d667-393f-56fd-ac89-764ecf509141/899.contextual_description: Bir Barruta is a historic well complex in Kairouan, traditionally attributed to the late AH 2nd / AD 8th century, and later to the AH 11th / AD 17th century, combining a venerated water source with architectural and hydraulic features. Housed beneath a domed chamber and operated by a camel-driven noria, it demonstrates the continuity of medieval water-lifting technologies and the spiritual significance attached to water in urban life, reinforced by legends linking its waters to Mecca.

6df2d667-393f-56fd-ac89-764ecf509141/dca.contextual_description: *Qanats* are ancient water systems devised in Iran that converted barren landscapes into fertile oases; they tapped into aquifers, using gravity to carry water from mountains and plains. While they were typically designed to provide fresh water for drinking and irrigation, this AH 6th-7th / AD 12th–13th century example was found inside the psychiatric hospital in the Norman capital of Palermo in Sicily.

6df2d667-393f-56fd-ac89-764ecf509141/968.contextual_description: *Sabil*s were repositories for drinking water only, not for collecting water for domestic uses. For the latter, Cairenes resorted to three sources of water: the closest canal or lake; water delivered by water carriers (if affordable); or a water seller who carried a container on his back.

6df2d667-393f-56fd-ac89-764ecf509141/76d.contextual_description: This AH 13th / AD 19th-century water seller’s jar from Egypt was designed for transporting and dispensing drinking water in urban settings. Combining an earthenware body that kept water cool through evaporation with a decorated copper-alloy upper section and a rope harness for carrying, it reflects the practical ingenuity and visual expression associated with the work of water sellers in everyday life.

6df2d667-393f-56fd-ac89-764ecf509141/c62.contextual_description: Used by *guerrab*s to transport and distribute drinking water in urban spaces, this traditional leather *gerba* from Marrakech predates modern water systems. Made of tanned goat leather and designed to keep water cool, it highlights the craftsmanship, mobility, and social role of water sellers in Moroccan daily life.

6df2d667-393f-56fd-ac89-764ecf509141/ed8.contextual_description: Constructed from wood covered with linen and a chalk ground, this ornate flask is enriched with gilding and painted decoration. Its surface shows scenes of lovers and musicians in a garden, imagery commonly used in Safavid art to convey refined leisure and elite court life. With its silk and silver-thread handle, the flask functioned both as a container and as an object of display, to be admired as much as used.

6df2d667-393f-56fd-ac89-764ecf509141/453.contextual_description: Called pilgrim flasks after similarly-shaped canteens used by pilgrims to hold holy water or oil, this glazed example from AH 6th / AD 12th-century Syria was used to hold drinking water. The loop and ring handles on each side of the neck would have held a strap to carry the vessel over one’s shoulder. This small flask was clearly designed for mobility, given its small size, handles, and that it was suspended for carrying.

2a31b6e0-43fa-5b33-af86-569f085568d3/3aa.contextual_description: Set within a bathhouse interior, this Persian miniature depicts figures engaged in washing and grooming. At the centre, Mihr is seated while attendants comb his hair, surrounded by others holding water bowls and tools. The arched interior and tiled walls frame the scene, presenting the bathhouse as a place of cleanliness, care, and social interaction.
